title: VPC/onprem install sanity sampler and hypothesis notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, pragmatic runbook intended for first-touch engineers who are called in during VPC or on-prem installation and early upgrade failures. It is intentionally terse — a sampler of quick hypotheses, prioritized probes, and short remediation actions that surface the most common runtime faults we keep seeing in customer installs (networking, TF state mismatches, driver/kernel issues, container image problems, and k/v cache corruption).

How to use this doc:
- Run the numbered probes in order (1..N) when you first get an incident.
- Each probe is fast (30s–5m) and gives high signal.
- Record outputs in the ticket. If a probe indicates a likely root cause, jump to the targeted remediation steps.

Quick TL;DR checklist (15–20 mins):
1) Can we reach the control plane? curl -sSf https://<control-plane-host>/health || note error
2) Is terraform applied and state consistent? terraform show on the operator machine
3) Are nodes healthy at the cluster level? kubectl get nodes, docker ps / crictl ps
4) GPU visible and drivers loaded? nvidia-smi or lspci | grep -i nvidia
5) Common logs: journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200; kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> -c runtime -f

Priority probes (order to run):
1) Control-plane reachability (networking) — 2m:
- Command: curl -v https://<control-plane-host>:443/health --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10
- Expected: HTTP 200 and small JSON {"status":"ok"}
- Failure fingerprints: TLS handshake timeout, "Connection refused", name resolution failures, or 502/503.
- Quick hypothesis: firewall/NACL or wrong DNS mapping (internal DNS override).
- Fast fixes: test from both jump host and from a worker node; verify DNS /etc/resolv.conf; check iptables/nft rules; port 443 allowed in security groups.

2) Terraform state and drift — 5–10m:
- Command: terraform init && terraform plan -detailed-exitcode (use the same workspace we used for apply).
- Expected: no drift, plan exits 0 or details indicate only harmless metadata changes.
- Failure fingerprints: provider plugin mismatch, missing module source errors, state locking (Error acquiring the state lock), resource not found errors referencing provider ids that differ from actual cloud resources.
- Hypotheses: partial apply, manual changes to infra, outdated provider versions.
- Fast fixes: unblock state lock (if stale) after confirming no live apply; run terraform providers lock file sync; roll forward provider version recorded in repo. If module missing: point module source to canonical repo commit used during initial deploy.

3) Node/runtime bootstrap & kubelet status — 3–8m:
- Commands (K8s): kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl describe node <node> | egrep "Kubelet|Network|DiskPressure|OutOfDisk"
- Commands (non-K8s installs): systemctl status redwood-agent; journalctl -u redwood-agent -n 200 --no-pager
- Expected: Ready state, kubelet health probes ok, agent active.
- Fingerprints: NotReady nodes, kubelet crashloop, long image pulls, mounting errors for /mnt/cache.
- Hypotheses: wrong kernel modules, missing sysctl settings, incompatible docker/containerd versions, underlying disk full.
- Fast fixes: restart kubelet/agent; check /var/log/messages for mount errors; verify container runtime version matches supported list and upgrade/downgrade temporarily (use apt/yum or host package manager).

4) GPU and driver smoke — 2–5m (only for GPU installs):
- Commands: nvidia-smi || cat /sys/class/drm/card*/device/uevent || dmesg | grep -i nvidia | tail -n 50
- Expected: nvidia-smi shows GPUs, driver version, process list.
- Fingerprints: nvidia-smi: "NVIDIA-SMI has failed because it couldn't communicate with the NVIDIA driver." or kernel oops/panic lines in dmesg.
- Hypotheses: driver mismatch vs kernel, secure boot preventing unsigned modules, firmware version mismatch.
- Fast fixes: ensure secure boot disabled or sign modules; reinstall driver matching distro/kernel; if using AMIs/host images, prefer our validated image tag.

5) Container images & registry issues — 3–10m:
- Commands: docker pull <image> or crictl pull <image>; kubectl describe pod <pod> to see ImagePullBackOff reasons.
- Expected: images pull normally, no 403/401 or timeouts.
- Fingerprints: 401 Unauthorized (registry creds), 404 (image tag missing), 504 (proxy/egress blocked).
- Hypotheses: blocked egress, expired registry token, private registry DNS.
- Fast fixes: test proxy bypass; validate registry credential secret in namespace; confirm image tag exists in registry UI.

6) KV cache and prefix cache corruption — 2–6m:
- Symptom: high latency with repeated token generation, OOMs in runtime, or odd hallucination errors during streaming.
- Commands: curl to admin cache endpoints on runtime (if enabled), look for metrics: cache_hit_ratio, kv_cache_size.
- Fingerprints: cache miss storms, rapid TTL eviction logs.
- Hypotheses: mismatched cache format across versions after upgrade, corrupted persisted cache files, or unexpectedly small cache allocation for workload profile.
- Fast fixes: flush cache (guided endpoint), bump cache memory temporarily in runtime config and restart, revert to pre-upgrade runtime that used older cache format if available.

Targeted remediation recipes (if a probe returns match):
A) Network path blocked between control plane and node:
- Confirm using traceroute and telnet on port 443 from node to control plane.
- If corporate firewall: ask networking team to add rule for control-plane CIDR; add explicit host entry in /etc/hosts as short-term mitigation.

B) Terraform plan shows provider mismatch:
- Lock to the provider version used at initial deploy: update required_providers in .tf and run terraform init -upgrade=false.
- If state references resource IDs that no longer exist, create a minimal stub resource or import the resource back into state (terraform import) only after confirming with owner.

C) Kubelet failing due to cgroup driver mismatch:
- Check container runtime's cgroup driver (docker info | grep Cgroup) and kubelet configuration. Align them (systemd vs cgroupfs) and restart services.

D) Runtime OOM/GPU OOMs after upgrade:
- Check dmesg for OOM kill logs, check runtime/worker logs for "out of memory".
- Temporary mitigation: reduce max_concurrency in runtime config, increase swap (careful on GPU hosts), or scale out worker pool by adding nodes to TF and triggering autoscaler.

Common error fingerprints & what they usually mean:
- "TLS handshake timeout" -> network path, MTU issues, or proxy breaking large handshakes.
- "state lock is held" -> leftover terraform lock; check who is doing apply; if stuck, run terraform force-unlock after confirming no active apply.
- "device not found" from runtime when creating GPU context -> driver not loaded or wrong PCI passthrough config.
- "ImagePullBackOff: unauthorized" -> registry creds or token expired.
- "failed to mount volume: no such file or directory" -> wrong hostPath in manifests, missing PV/PVC binding or permission mismatch.

Terraform module gotchas (notes for troubleshooting TF module problems):
- Our modules sometimes rely on implicit ordering that worked with earlier provider versions. If an apply partially succeeds and then fails on a later resource, secondary resources can be left in an inconsistent bootstrapped state. When you see partial resource creation, prefer terraform state rm (only if safe) or import to rehydrate state rather than manual cloud changes.
- TF remote state unlocks: we see CI apply bots time out leaving locks; standard policy: wait 10m for CI; otherwise escalate to infra lead and force-unlock with a note in ticket.
- Provider plugins: always run terraform providers mirror or use a pinned mirror used in CI; mismatched plugin versions are an 80% cause of weird plan diffs.

Upgrade preflight sampler (run before any runtime or control-plane version change):
- Take a snapshot of TF state and post it to ticket (terraform state pull > state-YYYYMMDD.json).
- Validate a small canary: modify a single node pool with new image tag in TF but plan only; run plan -detailed-exitcode.
- Run 'runtime --version' on a single node to confirm compatibility table.
- Run three small requests through a test route to confirm latency and correctness.

Observability quick hits (what to check in Console/Prometheus/Logs):
- CPU steal, disk i/o, network retransmits spike at install time = often underlying VM host noisy neighbor or misconfigured hosts.
- Token-level latency increase immediately after an upgrade = likely configuration mismatch with kv cache or batching defaults.
- Error budget burn for specific customer route = check rollout/fallback policy for that route in Console.

What to collect and attach to the ticket (minimum artifacts):
- Output of curl health endpoints (control-plane and runtime)
- terraform plan (text) and terraform state pull
- kubectl get pods -A -o wide and kubelet journal (last 500 lines)
- dmesg and nvidia-smi output (if GPU hosts)
- runtime logs (last 2000 lines) and runtime config file used
- any relevant cloud provider console screenshots showing resource state or quotas

Short runbook for on-call handoff (5 min):
1) State the hypothesis and what probe confirmed it.
2) Actions taken and immediate impact. 
3) What we changed in infra or config and why.
4) Reproduction steps and recommended next steps (rollback? additional tests?).

Notes / TODOs / Open questions:
- TODO: add a minimal shell script that runs the Priority probes and collates outputs (auth boundaries and secrets are the complexity).
- Open: define standard TTL for cache flush endpoints during upgrades (currently ad-hoc).
- TODO: canonicalize provider versions across private-deploy TF repos and put a CI gate that blocks upgrades if provider versions drift.

Appendix: useful one-liners
- Force-unlock TF state (use with extreme caution): terraform force-unlock -force <LOCK_ID>
- Dump kubelet config: sudo cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
- Quick check for disk pressure: df -hT | egrep "overlay|/var/lib"; sudo du -sh /var/lib/containerd/*
- Collect runtime logs into bundle: sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 5000 --no-pager > /tmp/runtime.log && gzip /tmp/runtime.log

End of document.
